items.title: Horizontal Translations of Quadratic Functions

sections.normalized_html: A curve is defined by [MATH: y = f(x),] where [MATH: f(x) = -x^2 + x + 2.] If [MATH: y = g(x)] is a horizontal translation of [MATH: y = f(x)] by [MATH: 2] units left, what is the function [MATH: g(x)?]
sections.readable_text: A curve is defined by [MATH: y = f(x),] where [MATH: f(x) = -x^2 + x + 2.] If [MATH: y = g(x)] is a horizontal translation of [MATH: y = f(x)] by [MATH: 2] units left, what is the function [MATH: g(x)?]

sections.normalized_html:
We're given the curve [MATH: y = -x^2 + x + 2] and we wish to translate this curve by [MATH: 2] units left.

For each point on the curve [MATH: y = f(x),] we must subtract [MATH: 2] from each [MATH: x]-coordinate to get the corresponding point on the new curve [MATH: y = g(x).] So, the [MATH: x]-coordinates of the points on the new curve are given by

[MATH: x_{\textrm{new}} = x - 2.]

This equation is equivalent to

[MATH: x = x_{\textrm{new}} + 2.]

To get the equation of the new curve, we substitute this into the equation of the first curve. Doing this, we get

[MATH: y|= − x^{2} + x + 2; y|= − (x_{new} + 2)^{2} + (x_{new} + 2) + 2.]

Dropping the [MATH: \textrm{new}] suffix, we get [MATH: y = -(x + 2)^2 + (x + 2) + 2.] Finally, simplifying the expression, we have [MATH: y|= − (x + 2)^{2} + (x + 2) + 2; y|= − x^{2} − 4x − 4 + x + 2 + 2; y|= − x^{2} − 3x.] Therefore, [MATH: g(x) = -x^2 - 3x.]

Item 8 — Example: Horizontal Translations of Quadratic Functions

Example Prompt:
A curve is defined by [MATH: y = f(x),] where [MATH: f(x) = -x^2 + x + 2.] If [MATH: y = g(x)] is a horizontal translation of [MATH: y = f(x)] by [MATH: 2] units left, what is the function [MATH: g(x)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We're given the curve
[MATH: y = -x^2 + x + 2]
and we wish to translate this curve by [MATH: 2] units left.

For each point on the curve [MATH: y = f(x),] we must subtract [MATH: 2] from each [MATH: x]-coordinate to get the corresponding point on the new curve [MATH: y = g(x).] So, the [MATH: x]-coordinates of the points on the new curve are given by

[MATH: x_{\textrm{new}} = x - 2.]

This equation is equivalent to

[MATH: x = x_{\textrm{new}} + 2.]

To get the equation of the new curve, we substitute this into the equation of the first curve. Doing this, we get

[MATH: y|= − x^{2} + x + 2; y|= − (x_{new} + 2)^{2} + (x_{new} + 2) + 2.]

Dropping the [MATH: \textrm{new}] suffix, we get
[MATH: y = -(x + 2)^2 + (x + 2) + 2.]
Finally, simplifying the expression, we have
[MATH: y|= − (x + 2)^{2} + (x + 2) + 2; y|= − x^{2} − 4x − 4 + x + 2 + 2; y|= − x^{2} − 3x.]
Therefore, [MATH: g(x) = -x^2 - 3x.]
